A page-order error costs almost nothing to make, is baked into the PDF, and is then
inherited silently by every note built from it. Eric's own framing: "cheap step, very
expensive mistake." He explicitly declined to cheapen the ingest itself, because that is
where judgement about what matters in the text happens.

**How to apply:**

- Build the artifact, then **verify by a route that shares no code path with how it was
  built.** For the book scan: the order was set by a *visual* read of cropped folio bands,
  so verification read the folio out of the *full-page OCR text* of the finished PDF, and a
  third pass rendered the PDF and read the folios off the rendered pages.

  duplicates == last − first + 1` costs nothing; make it a hard gate that refuses to
  proceed, and test it with a deliberately corrupted input. **But it is a map-consistency
  check, not a proof of order.** On the default path — where folios are assigned as a
  running counter — the two sides of the identity are equal *by construction*, so the gate
  compares a number with itself. A transposition, a wrong start page, a missed duplicate,
  and two cancelling errors all pass it.

  `verify_pdf.py` "checked" that folios increase by appending the *expected* value and
  testing that those increased — true by construction, so it printed YES unconditionally.

  and with the specific claims spelled out.

pass at reading page numbers off contact sheets, because the sheet prints the *expected*
number beside each crop — so the job is spotting disagreements, not reading every number.

mainly for speed; he was explicit that the savings are small and **the gate is the part
worth keeping.**

**What the gate actually caught, 2026-09-05.** The independent review returned **GO** on the
book PDF and **NO-GO** on the reference file shipped alongside it — which is the whole
argument for the gate in one result. It found: a verification check that was a tautology and
could never fail; an overstated claim about what the arithmetic gate proves; 7 chimeric
bibliography records welding one entry's authors to another's title; and 67 of 113 records

Here's how I'd approach the whole job.

## What's there now

Earlier I estimated a few hundred TB documents. The real size is much larger.

- **TB's Training Info** (Thomas Barbeau's shared folder): 2,179 files, 75 GB, about 80 coaches or systems. It holds 939 PDFs and about 610 videos. The biggest parts are:
  - SC Books (443)
  - Stop Chasing Pain (299 files, 28 GB, mostly video)
  - DNS (158)
  - David Grey Rehab (100)
  - Burdenko (91)
  - ALTIS (89)
  - ELDOA, Poliquin, Knees Over Toes, Natera Isometrics, KILO, Charlie Francis, and a long tail after that
- **Landon Evans:** about 800 files covering training books, physical preparation, science, therapy/rehab and nutrition.
- **Your Drive:** Old Bull, Harries RTP, CVASPS lectures, ALTIS/Clark, your own courses and manuals.
- **Other folders shared with you:** the monthly *Pro Football Sports Science Research Update* (about 10 issues), the 2026 CSCCa conference presentations, an Enoka ISB talk, and coach Lowe's drill folders.

That's roughly 5,000 or more knowledge files, over 700 videos, and a lot of duplicates. The same PDF shows up in three folders.

## The key idea: don't ingest everything

Reading all of it wouldn't turn me into your thought partner. It would turn me into a big search engine. The job has three layers, and only the third one makes me the partner you described:

1. **Catalog everything.** One list of every file: source, discipline, type and a fingerprint for spotting duplicates. A script does this, and it costs no model tokens.
2. **Deep-ingest a short, ranked list.** The sources you'd actually argue from.
3. **Write one synthesis note per discipline.** For example, hamstring rehab, where Harries, Landon, TB's David Grey folder and your own manual agree, where they disagree, and where you land. That's the layer that lets me push back on you with evidence.

## The pipeline

| Step | What | Cost | Tool |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | Manifest and duplicate removal across your Drive, TB, Landon and the shared folders | no tokens | PowerShell and gws (already working, shown above) |
| 1 | **Your baseline**: Playbook, Assessment Manual V12, HHPR 5355 transcripts, force plate protocols, Sportsmith articles | small, already text | Claude |
| 2 | Sort each item by discipline and value (A: deep-ingest, B: catalog only, C: skip) | cheap | Haiku and Codex in parallel |
| 3 | Route each tier-A item by type | varies | existing pipelines, below |
| 4 | Synthesis notes, one discipline at a time | the valuable part | Claude, with you reviewing |

**Why your own material comes first.** The whole point is to compare Landon, TB and Old Bull against how *you* already work. I can't do that until your method is in the system. It's also the easiest material to process, since most of it is already text.

**Where each type of material goes:**
- **Papers** go into Zotero. Zotero has only 861 of its 3,570 items full-text indexed, and 92 papers are waiting in the queue. Adding about 4,000 more PDFs now would bury that queue, so we clear it first.
- **Courses with transcripts** (Old Bull, Harries, HHPR) get broken into vault notes directly.
- **Books** go through `ingest-book`, but only after the check your review-gate note requires: an automated check, then an independent Codex review that tries to find mistakes.
- **Videos** go into a separate transcription queue. Local Whisper runs overnight on the Mac, and only for tier-A videos. Stop Chasing Pain alone is 28 GB.

## Rules I'll follow for safety and cost

- **Codex workers never point at the Drive.** Read-only access still means they can read, and your Drive holds DexaProject, Catapult exports and PFF data. Codex is an outside service. I'll copy each batch into a scratch folder and point Codex only there. I'll run one test batch first to confirm Codex's sandbox holds on Windows.
- **I'll take a snapshot of TB before ingesting.** You don't own that folder, and it was still being changed in August 2026. We ingest a fixed copy.
- **It all runs in the background during the season.** Small nightly batches, no heavy daytime work.
- **It's a long job.** Expect the catalog and your baseline in about a week. Each discipline after that takes a few sessions. The full set is months of background work.

## What only you can provide

The survey found **no written coaching philosophy anywhere**. That's the most useful thing you can add, more useful than any folder. It doesn't need to be an essay: 20–30 decision rules, like "when X, I do Y, because Z." I can pull them out of you with a short `/interview-me` session, one discipline at a time. That becomes the fixed point every source gets compared against.

## The decision I need from you

Your prioritization slate is full, **5 of 5** for Fall 2026: Tech Inventory, HPI Protocol, Education Curriculum, RTP CLA, and Women's Health. Your own rule is to name the trade-off before starting something new. The options:

- **A. Put it in the side lane** (outside the cap, by your choice). It runs as nightly background batches with no deadline or charter. This is my recommendation. It's how you're learning, not a staff deliverable.
- **B. Fold it into RTP_Constraints_Course** as that course's source base. That limits the first discipline to rehab and RTP, which is where your gap is biggest anyway.
- **C. Make it a charter project** and move something off the slate.

The first step (the catalog script) costs almost nothing, so I can build it under any of the three options. I'm holding off on setting up a repo or charter until you pick.

The Haiku search for Landon's loose files is still running, and its results will feed into the catalog. The Haiku TB search will likely come back empty, because TB isn't synced locally. That doesn't mean it's missing. The gws listing above is the real inventory.
